hook: The Portuguese captain who found the sea route from Europe to India.

pages.x: Vasco da Gama was born around 1469 in Sines, a fishing port in Portugal, into a minor noble family. Tough and hot-tempered, he was chosen by King Manuel I to finish what Prince Henry had begun: to reach India by sea.

He sailed from Lisbon in July 1497 with four ships. Swinging far out into the Atlantic, he spent three months out of sight of land, longer than any sailor before him, then rounded the Cape of Good Hope and sailed up the coast of East Africa.
At Malindi he found a pilot who knew the monsoon winds, and in May 1498 reached Calicut in India, the great spice port. Asked what they had come for, his men answered: "Christians and spices."

His gifts for Calicut's ruler were cloth, hats, coral, sugar and honey, and the court laughed: the poorest merchant brought better. Still, he sailed home with spices worth many times the cost of the voyage. Half his men died on the way, mostly of scurvy.

On his second voyage in 1502 he came with warships and bombarded Calicut. He captured a ship of Muslim pilgrims and burned it with hundreds of people on board. Portugal built forts along the coasts of Africa and India.
In 1524 he was sent back as viceroy of Portuguese India, but fell ill and died in Cochin on Christmas Eve, a few months after arriving.
Da Gama's voyage opened the first sea route from Europe to Asia. It tied the world's trade together by sea, and began centuries of European empire in Asia.
